title: Deciding What to Delegate
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece lays out a concrete process for figuring out which tasks to delegate, starting with a comprehensive personal task inventory that most leaders underestimate. It advises narrowing that list to repetitive tasks that don't rely on the leader's unique expertise, converting those into checklists (ideally created by the team member shadowing the leader first), and then separately identifying which remaining tasks would most accelerate a specific team member's growth. The essay pushes back on the common excuse that team members 'aren't ready,' calling it a cop-out, and reframes delegation as fundamentally a development tool rather than a workload-reduction tactic.
points: Recommends starting delegation decisions with a full personal task inventory, since most leaders underestimate how much they're actually holding onto.
Advises separating repetitive, non-expertise-dependent tasks (easiest to delegate first) from tasks requiring genuine unique skill.
Suggests having team members shadow the leader and build their own checklist, rather than the leader writing the process for them.
Directly challenges the common excuse that a team member 'isn't ready' for a task, calling it a cop-out that blocks growth.
Reframes delegation's primary purpose as team development, not workload offloading — a leader's job is to make others more skillful.
quotes: The first step in delegation is deciding what exactly to let others do, control, and own.
This can be a big list. So be sure not to skip over mundane and high-value tasks. You might be surprised at exactly how many tasks and projects you own and control.

Any task or project on your list that is highly repetitive is ripe for delegation. Repetitive tasks can be executed from a checklist or process that ensures quality, so creating a guide for execution allows them to be easily delegated to others.
It's too easy to imagine that team members aren’t ready to take on one of your tasks or projects, as they lack the experience to do things as well as you would. That’s a cop-out.
Your job as a leader is to make team members more skillful. You can’t achieve this without trusting those who aren’t perfectly ready for the challenge.
